Empirical Research Plan  
“International Trade and Income: Causal Evidence from Exogenous Shifts in Trade Costs, 1950-2015”

------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) with a gravity-based, shift–share instrument that exploits (i) time-invariant geography and (ii) time-varying, plausibly exogenous shocks to international shipping routes and transportation costs.

Why IV?  
• OLS estimates of the effect of trade on income are upward-biased if richer countries trade more (reverse causality) or downward-biased if protectionism increases when growth slows.  
• A DID/event-study around any single shock (e.g., containerization) would sharply cut the sample and treat all “high-port-depth” countries as homogeneous, leaving residual endogeneity.  
• A geography-interacted, time-varying trade-cost instrument—pioneered by Frankel & Romer (1999) and extended by Feyrer (2009)—delivers cross-country‐year variation that is powerful, transparent, and testable.

Construction of the instrument (Zct)  
Step 1: Compute bilateral “potential trade weights” ωcp = 1/Distcp × 1/BorderBarriercp (time-invariant).  
Step 2: For every year t, interact ωcp with exogenous, third-country demand Shockspt that come from:

 a. Technological shifts: the diffusion of containerization, measured by global container throughput in year t.  
 b. Geo-political route shocks: Suez closures (1967-75), Panama expansions (1963, 2016), Somali piracy (2008-12), etc.  
 c. World oil prices as a proxy for shipping cost shocks.

Step 3: Predicted openness for country c in year t:  

 Zct  =  Σp  ωcp × Shockpt

Because ωcp is fixed and only geography-based, the time variation comes solely from Shockpt, which is unrelated to any country-specific demand, supply, or institutional change in c.

------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
Trade openness, Tct = (Exports + Imports)/GDP, or log of real trade volume.

Control (counterfactual):  
Countries with identical geography (fixed distance network) but facing smaller exogenous changes in predicted trade costs at time t act as controls. The IV framework constructs this inside the regression; there is no single binary control group.

Treatment timing:  
Continuous—yearly shocks, 1950-2015.

------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 – Relevance: Geographic weights interacted with external shocks strongly predict actual trade openness. Testable in the 1st stage (F-stat > 10).  
A2 – Exclusion Restriction: Shocks to shipping routes affect a country’s income only through their impact on trade, not via other channels. Plausible because Suez closures, containerization, and global oil prices arise outside the domestic economy.  
A3 – Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-country spillovers beyond trade flows captured in Tct). Inter-dependence through global prices is limited given the small-open-economy assumption for most states.  
A4 – Time-varying common shocks are absorbed by year FE; country FE capture level-invariant geography and institutions.  
A5 – Linearity/log-linearity of the income–trade relationship (functional-form assumption). Checked via semi-parametric robustness.

Assessment: All assumptions are standard in the gravity-IV literature and reasonably plausible given the institutional context.

------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 – Violation of the exclusion restriction if shipping shocks influence income through energy prices or military conflict rather than trade.  
 Mitigation: Control for oil prices, regional conflict dummies; drop Middle-East oil exporters as robustness.

T2 – Measurement error in trade or GDP, creating attenuation bias and possibly weakening instruments.  
 Mitigation: Use multiple trade datasets (UN Comtrade, IMF DOTS) and Penn World Tables income series; instrument alleviates attenuation in the endogenous regressor; compare results across sources.

T3 – Global general-equilibrium feedback: A shock that raises world trade could directly raise world income, violating SUTVA.  
 Mitigation: Include year fixed effects, interact them with continent dummies, and perform leave-one-out (“jackknife”) IV that omits country c’s own shocks from Zct (Borjas, Freeman & Katz 1997 style).

------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Required packages
#------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-performance panel IV
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)
library(ggplot2)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
#------------------------------------------------------------
trade    <- fread("country_year_trade.csv")   # Exports, Imports
income   <- fread("country_year_income.csv")  # GDP, GDP per capita
distance <- fread("bilateral_distance.csv")   # Distance_ij, Border_ij
shocks   <- fread("external_trade_shocks.csv")# oil price, container index, route closures

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
#------------------------------------------------------------
## Trade openness
trade[, trade_open := (exports + imports) / gdp]

## Build fixed bilateral weights
distance[, weight := 1 / distance_km]
# Normalize weights to sum to 1 for each destination country
distance[, weight := weight / sum(weight), by = importer]

## Generate predicted trade openness (shift–share)
# Merge in time-varying external shocks (wide to long if needed)
# Assume 'shocks' has cols: exporter, year, shock_value
weights_shocks <- merge(distance[, .(importer, exporter, weight)],
                        shocks, by = "exporter", allow.cartesian = TRUE)

weights_shocks[, Z := weight * shock_value]
Zct <- weights_shocks[, .(Z = sum(Z)), by = .(country = importer, year)]

## Combine all
panel <- Reduce(function(x, y) merge(x, y, by = c("country", "year"), all = TRUE),
                list(trade, income, Zct))

## Additional controls
panel[, ln_pop     := log(population)]
panel[, ln_school  := log(1 + avg_years_schooling)]
panel[, ln_gdp_pc  := log(gdp_pc)]

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main 2SLS Regression
#------------------------------------------------------------
spec_main <- feols(ln_gdp_pc ~ trade_open + ln_pop + ln_school |
                   Z + ln_pop + ln_school |
                   country + year,
                   data = panel, cluster = ~country)

summary(spec_main)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check: Leave-one-out IV & dynamic leads/lags
#------------------------------------------------------------
panel[, Z_loo := Z - (Z * weight_self)]  # pseudo-code, weight_self = own weight
spec_loo <- update(spec_main, iv = ~ Z_loo)
summary(spec_loo)

# Dynamic event-study type (lead/lags)
for (k in -5:5) panel[, paste0("leadlag_",k) := shift(trade_open, k), by = country]
event_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("ln_gdp_pc ~", paste(paste0("leadlag_", -5:5), collapse=" + "),
        "| 0 | country + year"))
event_est <- feols(event_formula, data = panel, cluster = ~country)
iplot(event_est, ci = TRUE)

#------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Save output
#------------------------------------------------------------
etable(spec_main, spec_loo, file = "results_main.tex")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (gains-from-trade) predicts a positive effect. Prior evidence (Frankel-Romer, Feyrer) suggests an elasticity of 0.5–2.0.  I expect: a 10 percentage-point increase in trade openness raises GDP per capita by roughly 5 percent (elasticity ~0.5).

Distributional effects: mean income rises, but inequality may widen within developing countries; cross-country inequality likely narrows as poorer, trade-exposed countries grow faster.

------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)
------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (1)                 – strong 1st-stage F > 10 expected.  
C2: Exclusion restriction (0.5)              – plausible but not fully testable.  
C3: No simultaneous policy shocks (1)        – year FE & controls absorb.  
C4: Correct functional form (0.5)            – log/linear; semi-parametric tests pending.  
C5: SUTVA / no interference (0.5)            – some global spillovers unavoidable.

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 ⇒ acceptable but careful robustness required.

------------------------------------------------------------------
The proposed strategy leverages rich cross-country, over-time variation in exogenous trade-cost shocks to deliver credible causal estimates of how international trade affects income and growth.
